Multi-Physics Architecture

How to solve the same physical system using different mathematical representations.

What Are Formulations?

Formulation = choice of how to represent voltages and power flows

Same physics, different math, different numerical properties.

PowerInjection Formulation

Coordinates: Polar (θ, V)

Equations: P = f(θ,V), Q = g(θ,V)

Jacobian structure:

  • P depends more on θ
  • Q depends more on V

Use for: Most transmission systems (default)

CurrentInjection Formulation

Coordinates: Rectangular (Vr, Vi)

Equations: Ir = f(Vr,Vi), Ii = g(Vr,Vi)

Jacobian structure: More symmetric, better conditioned

Use for: High R/X ratios, stressed conditions, distribution networks

DCPowerFlow Formulation

Coordinates: Angles only

Equations: P = f(θ), voltages fixed at 1.0

Jacobian: Linear system

Use for: Fast approximations, thousands of scenarios, optimization

Why Formulations Are Types (Not Enums)

Each formulation is a Julia type:

struct PowerInjection <: FormulationTrait end
struct CurrentInjection <: FormulationTrait end
struct DCPowerFlow <: FormulationTrait end

Benefits

1. Type-based dispatch

# Compiler picks right method automatically
calc_residuals!(ws, pq, ::PowerInjection)   # Computes P, Q
calc_residuals!(ws, pq, ::CurrentInjection) # Computes I_r, I_i

2. Type safety

  • Can't mix PowerInjection workspace with CurrentInjection residuals
  • Compiler error if you try
  • Catches mistakes at compile time

3. Performance

  • No runtime checks ("if formulation == ...")
  • All dispatch at compile time
  • Each path gets specialized, inlined machine code

4. Extensibility

  • Add new formulation = define new type + implement methods
  • No modifications to existing code
  • No conditionals throughout codebase

5. Clarity

  • Function signatures show formulation-agnostic vs formulation-specific
  • Architectural dependencies visible

How Models Declare Multi-Formulation Support

Default Variables and Residuals

# PowerInjection formulation (default)
const PQ_VARS = [
    ModelVar(:theta, AlgebVar(), :Bus, :theta, :i, ...),
    ModelVar(:v, AlgebVar(), :Bus, :v, :i, ...),
]

const PQ_RESIDUALS = [
    ModelResidual(:p, AlgebRes(), SharedRes(), :Bus, :p, :i, ...),
    ModelResidual(:q, AlgebRes(), SharedRes(), :Bus, :q, :i, ...),
]

Formulation-Specific Overrides

# CurrentInjection formulation override
const PQ_VARS_CURRENT = [
    ModelVar(:v_r, AlgebVar(), :Bus, :v_r, :i, ...),
    ModelVar(:v_i, AlgebVar(), :Bus, :v_i, :i, ...),
]

const PQ_RESIDUALS_CURRENT = [
    ModelResidual(:i_r, AlgebRes(), SharedRes(), :Bus, :i_r, :i, ...),
    ModelResidual(:i_i, AlgebRes(), SharedRes(), :Bus, :i_i, :i, ...),
]

Registration in Metadata

function model_metadata(::Type{PQ})
    metadata = ModelMetadata(
        name = :PQ,
        vars = PQ_VARS,              # Default (PowerInjection)
        residuals = PQ_RESIDUALS,
        ...
    )

    # Register overrides
    metadata.vars_by_formulation[CurrentInjection] = PQ_VARS_CURRENT
    metadata.residuals_by_formulation[CurrentInjection] = PQ_RESIDUALS_CURRENT

    return metadata
end

Models without overrides: Only support default formulation.

Formulation Affects Variable Layout

Same system, different variables:

PowerInjection (14-bus system)

28 variables:
  θ[1..14] at addresses 1-14
  V[1..14] at addresses 15-28

CurrentInjection (same 14-bus system)

28 variables:
  V_r[1..14] at addresses 1-14
  V_i[1..14] at addresses 15-28

AddressManager must be formulation-specific because variable sets differ.

This is why AddressManager lives in ACPowerFlowProblem, not SystemModel.

Formulation-Specific Residual Dispatch

Signature includes formulation parameter:

calc_residuals!(ws, model, external, formulation::FormulationTrait)

Multiple Dispatch Selects Method

# PowerInjection implementation
@inline function calc_residuals!(
    ws::ResidualBuffers,
    pq::StructArray{<:PQ},
    _external::NamedTuple,
    ::PowerInjection  # Dispatch on formulation type
)
    pq_power_kernel!(
        (p = ws.res_vals.p, q = ws.res_vals.q),
        (pl = pq.pl, ql = pq.ql, ...),
        (v = ws.var_vals.v,),
        ws.active_mask,
        AT
    )
end

# CurrentInjection implementation
@inline function calc_residuals!(
    ws::ResidualBuffers,
    pq::StructArray{<:PQ},
    _external::NamedTuple,
    ::CurrentInjection  # Different formulation
)
    pq_current_kernel!(  # Different kernel, different physics
        (i_r = ws.res_vals.i_r, i_i = ws.res_vals.i_i),
        (pl = pq.pl, ql = pq.ql, ...),
        (v_r = ws.var_vals.v_r, v_i = ws.var_vals.v_i),
        ws.active_mask,
        AT
    )
end

Dispatch is automatic and type-stable:

  • Compiler knows formulation type at compile time
  • Right code path selected statically
  • No runtime branching

Adding a New Formulation

Steps:

1. Define Formulation Trait

# In src/foundation/traits.jl
struct MyFormulation <: FormulationTrait end

2. Specify Variables for Models

# For models needing different variables
const MY_MODEL_VARS = [
    ModelVar(:my_var1, AlgebVar(), :Bus, :my_var1, :i, ...),
    ModelVar(:my_var2, AlgebVar(), :Bus, :my_var2, :i, ...),
]

# Register in model_metadata
metadata.vars_by_formulation[MyFormulation] = MY_MODEL_VARS

Models using same variables as PowerInjection can skip this step.

3. Specify Residuals for Models

const MY_MODEL_RESIDUALS = [
    ModelResidual(:res1, AlgebRes(), SharedRes(), :Bus, :res1, :i, ...),
    ModelResidual(:res2, AlgebRes(), SharedRes(), :Bus, :res2, :i, ...),
]

metadata.residuals_by_formulation[MyFormulation] = MY_MODEL_RESIDUALS

4. Implement Residual Kernels

@inline function calc_residuals!(
    ws::ResidualBuffers{T, AT},
    model::StructArray{<:MyModel},
    _external::NamedTuple,
    ::MyFormulation  # Dispatch parameter
) where {T, AT}
    my_formulation_kernel!(
        # outputs, params, vars, active, AT
        ...
    )
end

Follow gather-compute-scatter pattern from existing models.

5. Test

prob = ACPowerFlowProblem(sys, MyFormulation())
sol = solve(prob, NewtonRaphson())

# Verify results match PowerInjection (if mathematically equivalent)
# Check Jacobian structure
# Verify convergence

AddressManager and workspaces handle your formulation automatically.

When to Use Which Formulation

PowerInjection (Default)

Good for:

  • Most transmission systems
  • Normal operating conditions
  • Matches engineering intuition

Why:

  • Equations naturally scaled
  • Jacobian structure exploited by sparse solvers

CurrentInjection

Good for:

  • High R/X ratios (distribution networks)
  • Systems with reactive compensation
  • Stressed conditions (large voltage variations)

Why:

  • Better conditioned equations
  • More symmetric Jacobian
  • Converges when PowerInjection struggles

DCPowerFlow

Good for:

  • Fast approximate solutions
  • Screening studies
  • Optimization (thousands of scenarios)
  • When reactive power doesn't matter

Why:

  • Linear system (no Newton iterations)
  • Much faster than AC formulations

Limitations:

  • Voltage magnitudes assumed 1.0
  • Reactive flows ignored

Architecture Summary

Key design decisions:

  1. Formulations are types - Participate in dispatch
  2. Models declare formulation-specific metadata - Variables/residuals per formulation
  3. AddressManager uses metadata - Allocates right variables
  4. Workspaces build buffers - Match declared variables
  5. Residual evaluation dispatches - To formulation-specific methods

Result:

  • Physical system (SystemModel) separate from math representation (formulation)
  • Solve same system multiple ways without changing data
  • New formulations integrate cleanly
  • Type system ensures safety, enables optimization

Example: Switching Formulations

using Powerful
using PowerFlowData

# Load system
case = PowerFlowData.parse_network("cases/ieee14.raw")
sys = SystemModel(case)

# Try PowerInjection
prob1 = ACPowerFlowProblem(sys, PowerInjection())
sol1 = solve(prob1, NewtonRaphson())

# Try CurrentInjection (same system, different math)
prob2 = ACPowerFlowProblem(sys, CurrentInjection())
sol2 = solve(prob2, NewtonRaphson())

# Results should be identical (mathematically equivalent)
v1 = get_var(sol1, :Bus, :v, (4001,))
v2 = get_var(sol2, :Bus, :v, (4001,))
@assert v1 ≈ v2

No model code changes. Just create new problem with different formulation.
